requirements.requirement: node1 (VyOS) routes between VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 via 802.1Q sub-interfaces
requirements.summary: eth1.10 (10.10.10.1/24) and eth1.20 (10.10.20.1/24) configured, committed, and saved on VyOS (cmd-293841069be94819, cmd-ada88899bf784b74); ip_forward=1 confirmed both pre- and post-restart (cmd-1f93867e0ff441f1, cmd-3ffd2a62ab634959).

requirements.requirement: node2 and node3 can still reach each other, routed through node1 (true VLAN segmentation, not flat bridging)
requirements.summary: Bidirectional pings between 10.10.10.2 and 10.10.20.2 succeed with TTL=63 (one router hop) both before and after restarts (cmd-8e2161815f5648bd, cmd-0ccb4c39ccee4502, cmd-f044fd1707614390, cmd-76afdd21b92c4527, cmd-95ff35fb34544096); tcpdump on node1 eth1 directly shows 802.1Q-tagged frames tagged vlan 10 arriving and being re-tagged vlan 20 by node1 and vice versa, proving genuine inter-VLAN routing rather than bridging (cmd-0a89ec05388d46b5).

requirements.requirement: Configuration persists across a reboot/restart of each managed node (VLAN interfaces, routes, and cross-VLAN connectivity recover automatically)
requirements.summary: All three nodes show a healthy pre-restart baseline with boot_id captured (cmd-c6fba7ee2da74d9d, cmd-70e66645ab41477d, cmd-a9b20a2b1c5f43b7), a restart acknowledgement and unreachability during the disruption (cmd-98895d3fdb754560/cmd-56285bac5fb048bf, cmd-6bac9718e5bd475f/cmd-6a48c2967f5a4b1b, cmd-893aad7a29f34ebc), a distinct post-restart boot_id (cmd-c447f54cedcc44aa, cmd-fc490ae15ba94bdd, cmd-757abd4960064803), and recovered VLAN interfaces, routes, ip_forward, and cross-VLAN ping (cmd-3ffd2a62ab634959, cmd-f044fd1707614390, cmd-76afdd21b92c4527, cmd-95ff35fb34544096). This is corroborated by the fixed lifecycle after_executor boot-identity snapshots matching the executor-captured post-restart boot_ids for all three nodes.

overall_summary: The executor successfully segmented node2 onto VLAN 10 and node3 onto VLAN 20 across the shared link, with node1 (VyOS) routing between them via 802.1Q sub-interfaces. Direct evidence includes tcpdump proof of tagged-frame re-tagging on node1 (not flat bridging), bidirectional cross-VLAN pings, and a full pre-restart-baseline/restart/post-restart-recovery cycle on all three nodes showing configuration persists across reboot. All material task outcomes are satisfied with strong, coherent evidence.
limitations: node2 and node3 VLAN configuration required multiple troubleshooting iterations (ifdown/ifup cycles, manual ip addr/route commands) before converging on the persisted interfaces.d config; the trace shows this converged correctly and was validated by an actual reboot, but the process was not clean.

Minor scratch files (/tmp/vlantap.log, /tmp/reboot.log, /tmp/tcpdump.pid) created during evidence collection were not explicitly confirmed removed; the bounded lifecycle temp-file diff does not include them so their final disposition is indeterminate.

operational_hygiene.summary: The core changes (VyOS vif config, /etc/modules and /etc/network/interfaces.d/*.cfg on the Ubuntu nodes) are correctly scoped to the task and confirmed to persist via the reboot lifecycle diffs, with no failed services, no package-health regressions, and no unrelated exposure changes in the after_executor snapshot versus after_prepare (only expected boot-id/socket-PID/tmp churn from restarts). However, node2 and node3 required an extended sequence of troubleshooting mutations to get the VLAN sub-interface address applied reliably: repeated ifdown/ifup cycles, manual `ip link del`, and several ad hoc `ip addr add`/`ip route add` commands issued outside the persisted config (cmd-8dbc9fc335614e9f, cmd-553fdc771b6a44bc, cmd-84719ffd7d14480b, cmd-a9d0e76644ac480b, cmd-fa752153d2704554, cmd-b9cd6df2018a4d49 on node2; cmd-1b83b442a19b4bd9, cmd-5dc47c87eb944e03, cmd-a64e701c29644ab9, cmd-e4d3781bf2074ea2, cmd-bb5abb819481456a on node3). These were bounded, non-destructive, and ultimately superseded by the persisted interfaces.d config, which is what was proven to survive the actual reboot -- so they left no incorrect residue, but they represent real trial-and-error against the live network state rather than clean single-shot configuration. Minor scratch files (/tmp/vlantap.log, /tmp/reboot.log, /tmp/tcpdump.pid) created for the tcpdump capture and reboot scheduling were not confirmed removed afterward, though they are low-risk and outside the bounded temp-file diff shown.
